svg.title: Paging with a paging cookie compared with simple paging
svg.desc: Left, paging with cookies: the client sends page 1 with count 500 and an order that ends with the primary key. The response contains 500 rows, MoreRecords true and a paging cookie that records the first and last row of the page. The client sends page 2 with the cookie unchanged; Dataverse starts directly after the last row. This repeats until MoreRecords is false. It is recommended for every data set size. Right, simple paging: the client sends only page number and count. For page 40 Dataverse reads all rows up to page 40, returns the last 500 and discards the rest, so each page is slower than the one before and the total is limited to 50,000 rows. A bottom strip lists the rules: do not combine top with paging, do not edit the cookie, order deterministically, and remember that QueryExpression adds no default order while FetchXML orders by primary key.
svg.text: Paging cookies keep every page fast; simple paging slows down and stops at 50,000 rows
Starts right after the last row.
… repeat until MoreRecords is false (no cookie on the last page).
Cost per page stays the same. Works for any number of rows.
A few queries return no cookie: then paging falls back to simple paging.
Request: page N, count 500, no cookie.
Each page is slower than the one
Fine for a small list with "jump to
page 3". Wrong for exports and jobs.
No top / TopCount together with paging • never edit the cookie • order by something unique last (the primary key) •
FetchXML adds an order by primary key when you give none; QueryExpression does NOT, so always add orders there.
